Title: Expanding youth mental health access through digital platforms
NewsSummary: Community dialogue in Kilifi highlights inclusive digital care
NewsContent:
​The Brain and Mind Institute (BMI) convened community health promoters and healthcare workers in Kaloleni, Kilifi County, on February 12, 2026, to share findings from a new study examining whether digital platforms can effectively deliver mental health support to young people in Kenya.

The research was conducted by Dr Moses Kachama as part of the Brain and Mind Institute’s Global Mental Health Postdoctoral Fellowship, a joint initiative with the Department of Global Health and Social Medicine at Harvard Medical School. The fellowship strengthens capacity in implementation science while supporting locally grounded research in low- and middle-income countries.

Bringing research into direct conversation with frontline providers, the forum focused on practical and scalable approaches for underserved communities.

The study titled Providing Mental Health Support to Young People in Kenya Through Digital Platforms: Is This an Acceptable Approach? explored the feasibility and acceptability of digital mental health interventions and gathered preliminary data to inform the co-design of a future digital programme tailored to Kenyan youth.

Findings reveal strong digital readiness among young people. Nearly three-quarters (73%) reported owning a personal digital device, while 17% accessed shared devices. More than 95% expressed openness to receiving mental health support through digital platforms.

However, important barriers remain. The high cost of devices and internet data continues to limit equitable access, particularly in rural and low-resource settings. Participants stressed that digital solutions must be designed with affordability and accessibility at their core.

“Young people are already active in digital spaces and are open to receiving mental health support online,” said Dr Kachama. “But for digital interventions to truly work, they must be affordable, guided by qualified mental health professionals and integrated with in-person services. That is how we ensure they remain safe, inclusive and responsive to young people’s real needs.”

After completing the first year of his fellowship at Harvard Medical School under joint mentorship from Harvard and AKU faculty, Dr Kachama returned to Kenya to implement the study in a real-world setting. The findings shared in Kilifi reflect this second phase, translating implementation science into community dialogue and action.

As mental health needs continue to rise among young people in Kenya, the study highlights a clear opportunity to harness digital platforms in ways that are affordable, inclusive and integrated with existing systems of care, bringing timely support closer to where young people live and connect.
